title: Tales of genetics: Bodybuilding Prodigy
summary: NH tells of an African immigrant housemate who ate greasy food without tracking, trained only about 40 minutes once or twice a week for four months a year using a random workout app, yet was as muscular and leaner than NH at 225 lbs. He attributes it to a naturally very high hormonal profile, notes the man refused free coaching because results came easily, and concludes that two years later NH's hard work surpassed him: hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard.

claims.claim: His housemate ate fried, greasy food and chips without counting calories, yet was ripped, dry and had very good muscle size.
At that time NH weighed about 225 lbs, bigger but much fatter than now, and was one of the biggest at his gym, training every day for about 2 hours.
The housemate trained about 40 minutes once or twice a week and not at all during the 8 cold months of the year.
His workouts came from a random workout generator app: burpees, sets of 25 with light dumbbells, no compound lifts, no heavy lifting, no progressive overload, no split.
Despite all that, NH admits the housemate would have beaten him on a natural bodybuilding stage at the time, a tough pill to swallow.
He offered to write a program and coach him for free to see his natural potential, but the man refused because results came easily and he lifted only to attract girls.
Talent is a double-edged sword: many extremely gifted people could go pro but don't care because it comes so easily.
He believes the man was natural; he didn't care enough to use PEDs, and his results came from a naturally very high hormonal profile.
He has met countless people with better bodybuilding genetics, but others being better doesn't mean you should quit; you can keep improving as long as you want.
After two years of hard work while the prodigy did random things, NH's physique now surpasses his: hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard.
